title: Let no one say it truly
hook: let no one be able to say truly that you aren't simple or good (Meditations 10.32)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was second edge: Marcus's question, is it this I'd miss, loosens the fear of death and sorts the hours. Your line was is it this.

Someone says something about you behind your back. Selfish, they say, or fake, or lazy. It stings, and soon you're arguing with them in your head, in the shower, on the drive. But there's a quieter question under the sting: is it true? Marcus doesn't tell himself to stop people talking. He tells himself something harder, and much more in his control.
screen: `SAID BEHIND YOUR BACK.` → `ARGUING IN THE SHOWER.` → `LET NO ONE SAY IT TRULY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Let no one be able to say truthfully of you, Marcus writes, that you are not simple, or not good. Let anyone who thinks that of you be a liar. Second, the shift. He isn't trying to control what people say. People will say what they say. He's trying to control whether it's true. You can't stop the rumor. You can make it false. Third, it's in your power. All of this, he writes, is up to you. Who can stop you from being good and simple? No one. Others can mislabel you, but they can't make the label stick to the person you actually are. Fourth, the test. When a remark lands, there are two questions. Is it true? If it isn't, it's their mistake, and you can let it go. If it is, even a little, you've been handed a free piece of information, and the work is to make it false. Either way, the energy goes into living, not defending. And notice his pair of words: simple and good, the same pair book ten opened with, when he asked his soul whether it would ever be good and simple. A few pages later, he's still working on it.
screen: `LET THEM BE WRONG ABOUT YOU.` · `YOU CAN'T STOP THE RUMOR.` · `WHO CAN STOP YOU BEING GOOD?` · `TRUE? THEN MAKE IT FALSE.` · then, large: `LET IT BE FALSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one criticism you've heard about yourself, or one you're afraid of, and ask gently whether there's any truth in it. If there's none, set it down. If there's some, picture the one act that would make it false: the generous thing for selfish, the plain thing for fake, the finished thing for lazy.
Two questions. Marcus's test for criticism: is it true, and if so, what will you do to make it false. Today's word.
Your line: let it be false. You can't stop the rumor, but you can make it untrue. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who use this passage often answer criticism by first asking whether it's true, and if any part is, by quietly changing that part rather than arguing.

chat.meaning: Marcus can't stop what people say, but he can make it false. If a remark holds some truth, the work is to change, not to defend.

Marcus.meaning: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations to himself

simple.meaning: Marcus's sense: single-hearted, one fold, nothing doubled over

book ten.meaning: the tenth of the twelve books of Marcus's Meditations

notes: 10.32 paraphrased (Long: 'Let it not be in any man's power to say truly of thee that thou art not simple or that thou art not good; but let him be a liar whoever shall think anything of this kind about thee; and this is altogether in thy power.
